input.question: Why is methionine always the "start" codon for proteins?
input.ground_truth: Interestingly, AUG is actually not the only start codon, though it is by far the most popular. [Alternative start codons](_URL_0_) include GUG and UUG. The most interesting thing is that these alternative codons are still translated as Met, regardless of what they typically code for, by using a special start codon tRNA. So, we come back to the same question: why Met? As far as I can tell, nobody really knows.

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: Why is methionine always the "start" codon for proteins?

Answer:

response.prediction:
Okay, let’s imagine you have a set of building blocks to make a big tower. But you need to know which block to put first to build the tower the right way.

In our bodies, proteins are like big towers made from tiny blocks called amino acids. But before we can start building, we need to know which block goes first. That’s where the "start" signal comes in.

Methionine is a special building block (amino acid) because it’s always the very first block in almost every protein tower we build in our cells. The cell has a tiny machine (called a ribosome) that reads instructions (called mRNA) to know which blocks to use and in what order. The instruction for "start here" is a special code, and when the ribosome sees it, it always puts methionine first.

So, methionine is always the first block because the cell’s instructions tell the machine to start building with it every time!
